Clarifying the concept

It's worth distinguishing three different things that often get conflated:

  1. Voluntary intermarriage, which rises or falls with social conditions and legal changes (e.g., after Loving v. Virginia in the US, 1967).
  2. State encouragement of mixing — propaganda, incentives, or immigration/settlement policies intended to promote blending.
  3. Enforced reproduction policies — coercive assignment of partners, forced removal of children, sterilization, or legal bans on endogamy.

The third category has essentially no serious contemporary advocates and has been implemented only in narrow, generally genocidal historical contexts. What follows describes the arguments that have been made, which is a different matter from whether they hold up.

Arguments advanced by proponents

The "no groups, no group conflict" premise. The core theoretical claim is that ethnic conflict requires distinguishable groups with distinct identities and boundaries. If phenotypic differences and separate lineages disappear, the argument goes, the raw material for categorization disappears too, and with it the basis for discrimination, segregation, and ethnic violence. This is a structural rather than attitudinal approach — it targets the existence of categories rather than trying to change how people feel about them.

Elimination of ascriptive inequality. Where wealth, status, and opportunity are distributed along racial lines and reproduced through inheritance within endogamous groups, universal intermixing would over generations dissolve the correlation between ancestry and life chances.

Kin-selection and contact reasoning. Some proponents drew on evolutionary or social-psychological ideas: if everyone has relatives of every background, in-group/out-group boundaries lose coherence, and the "contact hypothesis" operates at maximum intimacy — familial rather than merely social.

Hybrid vigor arguments. A recurring, biologically dubious claim held that mixed populations would be healthier or more capable. José Vasconcelos's La Raza Cósmica (1925) argued that a Latin American "fifth race" synthesizing all others would be spiritually and culturally superior. Richard Coudenhove-Kalergi made related speculative remarks in Praktischer Idealismus (1925).

Nation-building. Post-colonial and post-independence states often faced fragmentation along ethnic lines. Blending was framed as a route to a single national identity — Brazil's branqueamento and later "racial democracy" ideology, Mexico's mestizaje as official state doctrine, and Soviet theories of sliianie (the eventual "merging" of nationalities into a Soviet people).

What the historical record actually shows

The clearest case of genuine enforcement is Australia's "absorption" policy, associated with A.O. Neville and applied to Aboriginal people from roughly the 1900s–1960s. Mixed-descent children were forcibly removed from families and marriages were controlled with the explicit aim of "breeding out the colour." The 1997 Bringing Them Home report concluded this met the definition of genocide under the Genocide Convention (forcible transfer of children of a group with intent to destroy the group as such).

Notably, most historical blending programs were not egalitarian in intent. Mexican mestizaje and Brazilian branqueamento were widely understood as whitening projects — mixing was directional, meant to absorb and eliminate Indigenous and Black populations rather than create genuine parity. Vasconcelos's own writings contain explicit hierarchical assumptions. The Australian case was framed by administrators as a solution to an "Aboriginal problem," not as a favor to Aboriginal people.

Principal criticisms

Empirical. Conflict boundaries reassert themselves along other lines — language, religion, class, region, gradations of skin tone. Brazil and Mexico, the most-cited "success stories," retain strong colorism and steep racial stratification despite centuries of mixing. Rwanda's 1994 genocide occurred between groups that were genetically and linguistically indistinguishable, which directly undercuts the premise that physical similarity dissolves group antagonism.

Ethical and legal. Reproductive autonomy and freedom to marry are protected under Article 16 of the UDHR and Article 23 of the ICCPR. Coercive reproductive control constitutes a crime against humanity under the Rome Statute, and destroying a group's continuity as a distinct people falls within the Genocide Convention regardless of whether individuals are physically harmed. The policy asks a defined population to cease existing as itself — a cost that falls entirely on minorities, since majorities are demographically absorbed rather than erased.

The approach treats racial categories as biologically real objects to be manipulated, when the mainstream scientific view is that they are socially constructed classifications with weak correspondence to human genetic structure. If categories are constructed, they can be reconstructed around whatever markers remain.

Practical. Implementation would require a state apparatus capable of tracking ancestry, assigning partners, and punishing noncompliance — precisely the kind of racial bureaucracy the policy claims to abolish, and one available for repurposing toward hierarchical ends.

A note on the "Kalergi Plan"

Coudenhove-Kalergi's speculative writings have been extracted and reframed by white nationalist movements into a conspiracy theory alleging a coordinated elite scheme to eliminate white Europeans through engineered migration and intermarriage. No such plan exists; the theory has been repeatedly documented as a fabrication and has featured in extremist manifestos. If you encountered this topic through that framing, it's worth knowing that context.

Summary

The theoretical case rests on a genuine insight — group boundaries are prerequisites for group conflict — combined with several weak links: that the boundaries won't simply reform elsewhere, that biological mixing addresses socially constructed categories, and that a state coercive enough to implement it would remain benign. Historically, the actual implementations served assimilationist and eliminationist goals rather than egalitarian ones. Introduction
Racial divisions have long been a source of conflict, inequality, and systemic injustice. Despite progress in civil rights and multiculturalism, racial identity remains a potent and often polarizing force. This essay argues that governments should implement policies mandating interracial reproduction to eliminate distinct racial identities, thereby eradicating the social divisions they perpetuate. While controversial, this approach could accelerate the creation of a truly post-racial society, where superficial physical differences no longer dictate opportunity, perception, or belonging.

The Flaws of Racial Constructs
Race is a social construct with no basis in biological reality. Genetic diversity within so-called racial groups far exceeds differences between them, yet societies continue to ascribe significance to skin color, facial features, and ancestry. These arbitrary classifications fuel prejudice, discrimination, and systemic inequities. By mandating interracial reproduction, governments could dismantle the visual markers of race, rendering the construct obsolete. Over generations, a blended population would undermine the very concept of racial categories, making it impossible to sustain biases rooted in physical appearance.

Historical Precedents and Social Cohesion
Integration policies, such as school desegregation in the United States, demonstrate that forced proximity can reduce prejudice. Contact theory suggests that familiarity breeds acceptance, and interracial families inherently foster such connections. Children of mixed heritage often navigate multiple cultural worlds, acting as bridges between communities. A society where such blending is universal would see racial divisions replaced by shared human identity. Critics may cite failed assimilation policies, but these typically lacked the biological component necessary to dissolve racial boundaries permanently.

The most significant objection to this proposal is its infringement on reproductive autonomy. Others may fear authoritarian overreach, but safeguards could ensure policies are phased and voluntary where possible. The greater risk lies in maintaining the status quo, where racial hierarchies persist. A post-racial society would not be colorblind but unified, recognizing diversity without allowing it to divide.

Conclusion
The vision of a world without racial divisions is audacious but necessary. Government-mandated interracial reproduction offers a radical yet viable path to dismantling the artificial barriers that have plagued humanity for centuries. While the ethical and logistical challenges are substantial, the potential to eliminate racism at its root justifies bold action. By embracing this policy, societies can forge a future where identity is defined not by race but by our common humanity.

Such policies have been proposed or hypothesized in certain ideological writings (e.g., some 19th–20th century racialist literature, fringe eugenics, or occasional modern online manifestos), but they lack support from mainstream genetics, sociology, conflict studies, or public policy research. Below is a neutral summary of the claimed rationales that proponents have historically advanced, followed by the empirical and practical problems that have prevented their adoption by any democratic society or reputable institution.

Claimed rationales (as argued by proponents)

  1. Reduction of group conflict through elimination of visible “out-groups”
    Proponents argue that many ethnic or racial conflicts exploit visible physical differences as markers for in-group/out-group bias (a pattern documented in social psychology under “minimal group paradigm” and ethnic conflict studies). If distinct racial phenotypes were blended into a more uniform population over generations, the argument goes, it would become harder to mobilize one group against another on the basis of appearance alone. Historical examples sometimes cited include the long-term mixing in parts of Latin America, Hawaii, or certain post-colonial societies where hybrid identities correlated with lower salience of strict racial boundaries (though not with the disappearance of conflict).

  2. Supposed genetic “hybrid vigor” (heterosis)
    Some advocates invoke the biological phenomenon of heterosis, in which first-generation crosses between genetically distant populations can show increased height, fertility, or certain health metrics due to masking of recessive deleterious alleles. They extrapolate this to claim that widespread admixture would produce healthier, more robust populations and reduce the prevalence of population-specific recessive diseases (e.g., sickle-cell trait in some African-descended groups, Tay-Sachs in Ashkenazi Jews, cystic fibrosis in Europeans).

  3. Creation of a unified national or global identity
    In nationalist or cosmopolitan versions of the idea, a single “mixed” population is said to foster social cohesion by removing competing racial nationalisms. This has appeared in some Latin American mestizaje ideologies, early 20th-century “melting pot” rhetoric pushed to an extreme, or occasional science-fiction/world-government thought experiments. The claim is that loyalty would shift from race to culture, class, or civic identity.

  4. Moral or anti-racist framing
    A minority of proponents (usually in fringe online spaces) assert that because racism is partly rooted in observable difference, the most thorough way to “end racism” is to make racial distinction impossible through enforced mixing. They sometimes compare it to historical policies that discouraged cousin marriage or tribal endogamy to reduce clan feuds.

Factual and empirical problems with these claims

  • No modern democratic state has ever implemented “enforced interracial reproduction.”
    Coercive mating programs (whether by quota, incentive, or punishment) are widely regarded as gross violations of bodily autonomy, reproductive rights, and international human-rights norms (see UN conventions on genocide, forced assimilation, and reproductive freedom). Past authoritarian regimes that attempted large-scale social engineering of identity—e.g., certain colonial “civilizing” projects, Soviet nationalities policy, or explicit racial programs in the 20th century—produced backlash, not stable harmony.

  • Genetics does not support “blending into one identity” as a conflict cure.
    Human genetic variation is clinal and mostly within, not between, classically defined races (Lewontin 1972; Rosenberg et al. 2002). Admixture increases heterozygosity but does not eliminate ancestry-correlated variation; principal-component and admixture mapping still recover continental-scale clusters even in heavily mixed populations (e.g., Latin America, African Americans). Visible traits (skin color, hair texture, facial morphology) are polygenic and can re-segregate under assortative mating, which is common even in diverse societies. “Hybrid vigor” is real in some traits and environments for first-generation offspring but tends to dissipate in subsequent generations; long-term outbreeding can also disrupt locally co-adapted gene complexes.

  • Empirical record on diversity and conflict is complex.
    Comparative studies (e.g., Easterly & Levine 1997; Alesina et al. 2003; Putnam 2007; Fearon & Laitin) show that ethnic fractionalization correlates with lower trust, poorer public goods provision, and higher risk of conflict under certain conditions (especially when ethnicity is politically mobilized). However, the causal direction is debated, and many highly diverse societies maintain stability through institutions, cross-cutting identities, and economic opportunity. Conversely, some of the most genocidal episodes in history occurred among genetically and culturally similar groups (Rwanda, former Yugoslavia, Cambodia). Visible racial blending has not been shown to be either necessary or sufficient for peace.

  • Sociological and psychological findings.
    Implicit-bias and minimal-group experiments demonstrate that humans readily form in-groups on trivial or arbitrary bases once visible racial cues are absent (Tajfel, Sherif, Kurzban et al.). Reducing phenotypic difference might simply shift conflict to linguistic, religious, class, or ideological lines.     Enforcing reproduction by race requires classifying citizens racially, tracking mating, and applying state coercion—measures incompatible with liberal democracy and easily abused.
